title: Gold hits one-week high, set for weekly gain as oil slide eases inflation fears
excerpt: Spot gold rose 1.2% to $4,390.11 an ounce on Friday, its highest since September 11, as a third straight drop in crude prices cooled inflation worries — though a strong dollar and hawkish central banks capped gains.
body:
• Spot gold rose 1.2% to $4,390.11 per ounce on Friday, its highest since September 11, putting bullion on track for its first weekly gain in four, up about 1% for the week.
  • Brent crude fell for a third straight session as fears of Saudi supply disruptions eased, cooling inflation worries and forcing a rapid unwinding of short positions in gold.
  • Gains were capped by a dollar at a more than seven-week high and hawkish central banks: the Federal Reserve raised rates to 3.75%-4% on Wednesday, and the Bank of Japan lifted rates to a 31-year high.
  • Silver, platinum and palladium all advanced more than 1.5% on the day, with each metal also headed for a weekly gain.

Gold snaps three-week losing streak

Gold prices climbed to a one-week high on Friday and were on track for their first weekly gain in four, as lower oil prices eased concerns about prolonged inflationary pressures, according to Reuters.

Spot gold was up 1.2% at $4,390.11 per ounce by 2:14 p.m. EDT (1812 GMT), after touching its highest level since September 11 earlier in the session. Bullion has gained about 1% so far this week. U.S. gold futures settled 0.6% higher at $4,424.90.

Brent crude extended its losses for a third straight session as easing concerns over Saudi supply disruptions outweighed anxiety about a widening conflict across the Middle East.

"Easing of oil prices reduces inflation pressures as oil has been the main driver of overall inflation... Precious metal investors had expected a (U.S.) rate hike and piled into short positions to take advantage of the expected selloff in gold. These positions have been rapidly unwound."

— Chris Gaffney, president of world markets at EverBank

Context & Background

The rally comes in the wake of an aggressive week from global central banks. The U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point to the 3.75%-4% range on Wednesday and flagged more hikes in the coming months. Traders now see a 55% chance of another U.S. rate hike when policymakers meet next in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Although gold is traditionally viewed as an inflation hedge, higher interest rates can diminish its appeal by making yield-bearing assets more attractive. The Bank of Japan joined the tightening push, raising interest rates to a 31-year high and signaling its readiness to keep pushing up borrowing costs. Meanwhile, the dollar rose to a more than seven-week high, making greenback-priced bullion more expensive for holders of other currencies — a headwind that limited gold's advance.

Goldman Sachs said in a note that it expects "the impact of tighter monetary policy to be felt primarily through a slower near-term appreciation path rather than a lower terminal gold price."

Impact & Analysis

After betting against gold ahead of the Fed's decision, traders reversed course as oil's slide took the heat out of the inflation outlook.

"The precious metal appears to have taken the Fed's hawkish signals in stride, instead finding immediate relief from falling oil prices amid hopes that the Fed's hiking cycle will prove shallow," said Han Tan, chief market analyst at Bybit.

The rally extended across precious metals. Spot silver rose 2.3% to $66.70, platinum gained 2.2% to $1,812.50 and palladium added 1.5% to $1,310.20, with all three metals also headed for weekly gains. Traders are watching the $4,400 to $4,440 zone as the next technical hurdle for gold: "Gold is currently testing resistance near the $4,400 to $4,440 range and a move above this resistance level could clear a path higher for gold prices," Gaffney said.

Diaspora Angle

Physical gold demand in India — the world's largest consumer market — was subdued this week as buyers held back purchases in anticipation of lower prices, while premiums in China remained steady, supported by robust investment demand, according to Reuters. For diaspora households that track gold prices ahead of festival and wedding-season buying, the soft patch in physical demand may mean retailers start quoting keener rates as the season approaches.

What's Next

Whether gold can break through $4,400 will depend largely on what happens in the Middle East and at central banks.

"Looking ahead, the state of the conflict in the Middle East will be a key factor influencing gold prices. If the conflict prolongs and oil prices remain high well into next year, that could prompt central banks to raise rates more than investors expect, which would put downward pressure on gold prices."

— Hamad Hussain, climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics

For now, markets see a Fed hiking cycle that may prove shallow and an energy market where supply fears are fading rather than building — the combination that snapped gold's three-week slide.
